matching.reasoningTemplate: Acute hypotension with urticaria/angioedema and bronchospasm after exposure indicates anaphylaxis.

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e Ch. 364 (Anaphylaxis), pp. 2812-2814; distributive-shock context p. 2358
clinicalPearls: Onset is typically within seconds to minutes of exposure to the trigger; an exception is the delayed (about 3-6 h) reaction to mammalian meat seen in alpha-gal syndrome (p. 2812-2813).
Most episodes (about 80-90%) are uniphasic, but roughly 10-20% are biphasic, with symptoms recurring an hour or more after the initial reaction has resolved (p. 2812).
Cutaneous features (urticaria, flushing, generalized warmth) are the most common manifestation, present in over 90% of cases (p. 2812).

Cross-linking of allergen with IgE bound to FcepsilonRI receptors on mast cells and basophils is the usual initiating mechanism; sensitization requires prior exposure, so repeated exposure to the antigen is a key risk factor (p. 2812-2813).

Some severe reactions are non-IgE-mediated and can occur on first known exposure, because direct mast-cell activation needs no prior sensitization (e.g., via the MRGPRX2 receptor with neuromuscular blockers, quinolones, and icatibant) (p. 2813).

Severe Hymenoptera sting anaphylaxis, especially with prominent hypotension, may be the first presentation of underlying systemic mastocytosis; checking a baseline tryptase screens for this (p. 2812-2813).
Failure to give epinephrine within the first 20 minutes of symptoms is a risk factor for poor outcomes (p. 2813).

About 6% of Western populations carry hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, an extra TPSAB1 allele giving a high baseline tryptase that can confound interpretation and may itself be a risk factor for severe reactions (p. 2813).
harrison.pathophysiology: Anaphylaxis is driven by mediators released chiefly from mast cells, basophils, and eosinophils. The most common mechanism is allergen cross-linking of IgE bound to FcepsilonRI on mast cells and basophils, triggering degranulation. Preformed granule contents include histamine, proteases (tryptase, chymase), proteoglycans (heparin, chondroitin sulfate), and TNF-alpha; newly generated arachidonic-acid products include cysteinyl leukotrienes, prostaglandin D2, and platelet-activating factor (PAF). Histamine produces flushing, urticaria, pruritus and, at high levels, hypotension and tachycardia; cysteinyl leukotrienes and PGD2 cause bronchoconstriction and increased microvascular permeability, with PGD2 also recruiting eosinophils and basophils. Serum PAF correlates with severity and is inversely related to PAF acetylhydrolase. Tryptase and chymase activate complement (generating the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a) and the kallikrein-kinin system, with mediator effects likely additive or synergistic. Reactions can also be non-IgE-mediated: direct mast-cell activation (e.g., via MRGPRX2 by neuromuscular blockers, quinolones, icatibant; or opiates, vancomycin, radiocontrast, NSAIDs), complement activation (e.g., Cremophor-solubilized paclitaxel), or contact-system/bradykinin generation (e.g., oversulfated chondroitin sulfate heparin contaminant). (p. 2812-2813)
additionalDifferentials: Systemic mastocytosis (elevated baseline tryptase; spindle-shaped mast cells on bone marrow) (p. 2813)
Systemic capillary leak syndrome (severe hypotension with poor response to first-line agents) (p. 2813)
nonInfectiousMimics: Scombroid poisoning (ingested histamine from improperly stored histidine-rich fish such as tuna, mackerel, mahi-mahi); clinically mimics anaphylaxis but tryptase is NOT elevated because histamine is exogenous, and skin test/oral challenge to fish are negative (p. 2813)

Direct (pseudoallergic) mast-cell degranulation from opiates, neuromuscular blocking agents, vancomycin, or CT radiocontrast (e.g., via MRGPRX2) - clinically indistinguishable from IgE-mediated reactions but occurs without prior sensitization (p. 2813)

Vasovagal (neurally mediated) syncope - provoked by emotion, pain, or orthostatic stress and accompanied by bradycardia, in contrast to the tachycardia and urticaria/angioedema of anaphylaxis (p. 2813; cf. p. 156-157)
additionalInvestigations: Serum tryptase peaks 60-90 min after onset and remains measurable for up to about 5 h; apply the '20% + 2' rule (an acute level >20% above the patient's baseline plus 2 ng/mL is diagnostic of clinically significant mast-cell activation) (p. 2813)

Repeat tryptase once the patient is stable to establish the individual baseline, since baseline serum tryptase varies widely and can be raised by hereditary alpha-tryptasemia or high environmental allergen exposure (p. 2813)
Serum histamine is of limited use acutely - its measurable window expires within about 1 h of onset (p. 2813)
Allergen-specific skin testing or serum-specific IgE to confirm a suspected drug or food trigger (p. 2813)
Baseline tryptase in sting-induced anaphylaxis to screen for underlying systemic mastocytosis (p. 2813)
redFlags: Hypotension or hypoxia - the most dangerous features, risking cardiovascular collapse or respiratory failure (p. 2812)
Laryngeal edema (sensation of a lump in the throat, hoarseness, stridor) or angioedema of the epiglottis/larynx threatening mechanical airway obstruction (p. 2812)
Bronchial obstruction (chest tightness, wheezing), especially severe in patients with underlying asthma, who have increased mortality (p. 2812)
Underlying asthma or cardiovascular disease - predisposes to more rapid decompensation (p. 2812)
Severe GI involvement (vomiting, crampy abdominal pain); bowel-wall angioedema can deplete intravascular volume enough to cause cardiovascular collapse (p. 2812)
harrison.prognosis: Severe and even fatal complications can develop within minutes of symptom onset, making early recognition critical; deaths occur via airway/bronchial obstruction, laryngeal angioedema, or vascular collapse. Delaying epinephrine beyond the first 20 minutes worsens outcomes. Risk is higher with underlying asthma or cardiovascular disease. Natural history varies by trigger: most childhood egg, milk, soy, and wheat allergy resolves, whereas about 80% of peanut allergy persists for life. (p. 2812-2813)
pitfalls: Treat with epinephrine first - antihistamines, glucocorticoids, and bronchodilators are ancillary agents for residual urticaria/angioedema and bronchospasm once the patient is hemodynamically stable, not initial therapy (p. 2813).
Biphasic reactions in 10-20% recur an hour or more after apparent recovery, so a period of observation is needed after initial resolution (p. 2812).

A normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis - it is not elevated in scombroid poisoning (exogenous histamine), and an acutely 'normal' value may still be diagnostic relative to a low individual baseline (apply the 20% + 2 rule) (p. 2813).
Non-IgE-mediated reactions can occur on first exposure, so the absence of prior exposure does not rule out an anaphylactic reaction (p. 2813).
Beta blockers can blunt the response to epinephrine; consider an alternative antihypertensive in patients at high risk of needing emergency epinephrine (p. 2813).
Skin/serum specific-IgE testing to foods has relatively poor predictive value, so a positive test alone does not confirm clinical reactivity (p. 2814).
